title: Flash Eurobarometer 578
text:
About the survey
Main aim. To identify what drives and what hinders the adoption of AI and
algorithmic management in smaller companies, with a focus on workplace
issues.
Also covers. Workforce uses (recruitment, HR decisions, performance monitoring,
scheduling, health and safety, training), human oversight, expected
effects on job quality (job satisfaction, safety, privacy, workload),
employees’ reactions as seen by employers, motivations such as labour
shortages, and barriers. No questions on employment or productivity
effects.

title: EIB Investment Survey
text:
Results

The EIB labels this chart “Firms using generative AI”, and the note under it lists two questions: whether the firm uses big data analytics and artificial intelligence, and whether it invests in generative AI tools (overview, p. 27). The EIB does not say how the two answers are combined. The sector figures suggest a firm must answer yes to both: 39% of manufacturing firms and 36% of service firms are counted here, while 48% and 41% use big data and AI (p. 25), and a measure counting a yes to either question could not be lower than that. Shares are weighted by value added (“About this publication”), whereas Eurostat’s 20% for 2025 counts each firm equally; Bick et al. find that reweighting Eurostat’s data by value added gives levels close to the EIBIS ones (St. Louis Fed Working Paper 2026-003B, Section 3.2 and Appendix C.1; the NBER version, w34995, does not include this comparison).

About the survey
Main aim. To monitor working conditions and job quality across Europe. The AI
question is one item in a long questionnaire on tasks, autonomy, work

title: Eurofound EWCS
text:
Results
12% of EU workers use generative AI tools at work. Among EU countries the share runs from 5% or less in Greece, Italy, Portugal and Romania to at least one in five in Luxembourg, Sweden, Belgium and Denmark (Eurofound overview report, pp. 27-28). Across all 35 countries surveyed, the range is from under 3% (Bosnia-Herzegovina) to about 25% (Luxembourg).

title: Company surveys
text:
McKinsey
The state of AI in 2026: On the road to ROI Firm · McKinsey & Company · 4 May to 8 June 2026 · Organisations, as reported by 1,719 respondents at all levels in 97 countries answering an online survey about their organisation; 36% work for organisations with more than $1 billion in annual revenue; weighted by each country’s share of global GDP. Asks whether the organisation regularly uses AI in at least one business function; exact wording not published.
In 2026, 89% of respondents said their organisation regularly uses AI in at least one business function, against 88% in 2025 (Exhibit 1). Among organisations using AI, 44% are scaling it across the enterprise, up from 38%. The 2026 report gives no results by region. The Stanford AI Index 2026 publishes McKinsey’s 2025 results by region (Figure 4.3.2, p. 194): Europe 91%, up from 80% in 2024 and 57% in 2023, although before 2025 McKinsey asked about adoption rather than regular use. Respondents are not a representative sample of firms and any regular use in a single function counts, so the share is far above the 20% of EU enterprises with 10+ employees in Eurostat’s 2025 survey.


The 2026 survey asked respondents whose organisation regularly uses AI how AI changed total employment over the past year: 14% report a decline, less than half the 32% who expected one in the 2025 survey, and two-thirds report little or no change (Exhibit 16).

title: ECB Corporate Telephone Survey
text:
About the survey
Main aim. To gather early information on business conditions from large euro area
companies the ECB is in regular contact with. This one-off survey of the
same contacts asked about labour market trends and the adoption of
generative AI.
Also covers. Labour shortages and difficulty recruiting (scarce skills, changing
skill needs, wages), labour hoarding, hours worked and remote working.
No AI results are published by sector, size or country.

title: ECB Corporate Telephone Survey
text:
Results
Almost three-quarters of the firms say they already use generative AI in their operations, but about half estimate that no more than 10% of their workforce uses it at least once a week, and only 6% put that share above 25%. Improving employees’ access to information is the main motivation, rated important by more than 90% of users, closely followed by producing content, developing software and engaging with customers; around half of users also see reducing headcount as an important motivation. The firms are among the largest in the euro area, so the share is far above estimates for all firms, and it is not plotted on the overview. The ECB Blog of 28 March 2025 summarises the same results.
